content: 1. Due to the very low rate of events, the evidence is limited in its reliability and interpretability. 2. The systematic review does not provide absolute values; therefore, data were abstracted from the post hoc ONTARGET analysis. 3. When assessing the certainty that there is no significant effect (using a threshold of 10 per 1,000 patients), the 95% confidence interval (CI) crossed this threshold, indicating the possibility of both significant harm and benefit. 4. For myocardial infarction, cognitive impairment/dementia, heart failure events, and blood pressure (BP) reduction and control, no data were reported. 5. The co-primary endpoints were defined as a composite of cardiovascular events and achieving target BP. 6. The confidence interval for certain outcomes crossed the line of no effect, suggesting that the observed differences could be significantly less or more impactful. 7. The included trial was judged to have a high risk of bias in the domains of participant and personnel blinding. 8. The baseline risk was extracted from the COPE 2013 trial. 9. The certainty of no significant effect was rated using a threshold of 10 per 1,000 patients, but the upper end of the 95% CI crossed this threshold, suggesting potential harm. 10. Stroke, cognitive impairment/dementia, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and BP reduction/control were not reported in the data. 11. The systematic review relied on indirect comparisons from network meta-analyses for certain outcomes. 12. The review did not provide I-squared values or confidence intervals for individual studies to assess heterogeneity. 13. The review used a loop-specific inconsistency approach to evaluate discrepancies between direct and indirect evidence, with results considered non-significant if the 95% CI of inconsistency factors included zero or if the ratio of odds ratios (RoR) included one. 14. A 50% drop in eGFR and doubling of serum creatinine were considered validated surrogate markers for end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). 15. Imprecision was downgraded due to the low number of events. 16. The systematic review did not provide weights for included studies or perform a risk of bias assessment. 17. The ALLHAT trial's amlodipine arm was double-counted in the review, which could have artificially narrowed the 95% CI. 18. The dominant trial had missing data, and the review was of low quality, lacking a risk of bias assessment. 19. Point estimates varied significantly in direction and magnitude of effect, and statistical tests for heterogeneity were not reported. 20. The PREMIER study, which contributed significant weight to pooled effect estimates, was judged to have a high risk of bias due to incomplete outcome data. 21. Serum creatinine and creatinine clearance were used as surrogate markers for ESKD, but indirectness was downgraded due to the population not being representative of the general hypertensive population. 22. The two trials contributing most of the weight to pooled estimates were conducted in diabetic patients, leading to a downgrade in indirectness. 23. No statistically significant differences in the risk ratio (RR) of adverse events were observed between men and women. 24. The confidence interval crossed the lower limit of 5 mmHg for BP reduction, requiring further review by the panel. 25. The systematic review did not provide weights for included studies, and some studies were judged to have a high or unclear risk of bias in the domains of blinding and incomplete outcome data. 26. The review did not meet the optimal information size due to the low event rate. 27. The two trials contributing most of the weight to pooled estimates were judged to have a high risk of bias in multiple domains, including allocation concealment, blinding, and incomplete outcome data. 28. The three trials contributing most of the weight to pooled estimates were judged to have a high risk of bias in similar domains. 29. The point estimates varied significantly in direction and magnitude of effect, and statistical tests for heterogeneity were not reported.
